plain: Lovable is a website where you write in plain English what you want to build and it puts the app together in front of you: the screens, the buttons, the forms, and the place where what people type gets saved. It doesn't give you instructions so you can do it yourself, and it doesn't hand you code to copy: it builds it and shows it to you working in the right half of the screen. You look at it, tell it in plain language what's wrong, and it changes it. The honest comparison: asking a chatbot for code is having someone explain over the phone how to assemble furniture; this is having someone come over, assemble it in your living room, and ask if you want it more to the left.

account.free: There's a free plan and it's good enough to really try it out: it gives you a handful of messages a day, enough to put up a first screen and tinker with it. Careful how it's billed, because it's not like a normal subscription: here you don't pay by time or by project, you pay in CREDITS, and every instruction you send uses one up. Five loose corrections like 'make it bigger', 'now blue', 'now centered' cost five times more than one well-written message. Paid plans ran around $25 a month for the entry tier as of August 2026, with higher tiers depending on how many credits you need. Check for yourself at lovable.dev before paying: these tools change prices and plan names every few months, and I don't want to give you a stale number.
steps: Type it directly into your browser's address bar. Watch out for sponsored search results: there are clones circulating with similar names that ask for a card from minute one. The real site is lovable.dev, nothing before or after it.

It's at the top right and says 'Sign up', next to 'Log in', which is for signing in with an account you already have. Signing in with Google is the fastest way and saves you from inventing another password.
The free plan is available from the very first moment and doesn't ask for one. If at any point it asks for one to 'verify', stop and check that you're on lovable.dev and not on an imitation.

Click your avatar at the top right and go into account settings. Find the plan section. Note two things before writing anything: how many messages you get a day and what time they reset. Knowing you have five attempts completely changes how you write the first one.

There's a GitHub button in the project menu. If you don't have an account, create one: it's free and takes two minutes. You don't need to understand what it is yet. All you're doing is making sure your work also exists outside this website, so that if prices go up tomorrow, they shut down, or you get tired of it, any programmer can pick up what's there and continue. It's the difference between renting and owning the deed.
Write your brief before opening the text box

On paper: who's using it, what they see, what they can do, what happens next, and how you'll know it worked. Five lines. This isn't bureaucracy: it's half the work, and it's what separates an app that resembles what you wanted from a generic one that then takes ten messages to straighten out.
account.warning: Until you set up user accounts, your app is open to anyone with the link, and Lovable won't remind you of that. Don't put a single real customer detail in there 'just to test': a real person's name and phone number on a public screen is a real problem, not a test. To test, make up the data.

first: Write down on paper what you want to build, in five lines and without a single technical word. This paper is what you'll paste in later.
Send a single long message with the whole brief, and end it by asking it to tell you what it understood and what it had to assume before building anything.
Read the list of assumptions. There, in black and white, you'll see everything you hadn't explained well. Fix only that, without using the chance to ask for new things.
Once it's built, use it the way your customer would: fill it in, submit it, upload something. Then break it on purpose: submit it empty, type a hundred-letter name.
Open it on your actual phone. Half your users will come in from there, and screens that look perfect on a computer often break on a narrow screen.
shortcuts: The chat box, on the left

This is where you talk to it. Everything you type there costs a credit, so think before writing. The rule that saves the most credits: bundle five corrections into one numbered message instead of sending five messages.
The preview, on the right
Your app actually working, not a drawing: you can click, fill it in, and break it. This is where you should be working; looking at the code is a distraction during your first sessions.
The project's undo button (version history)
Every change gets saved as a version you can go back to. It's your safety net when a change made three things worse at once. Find it before you need it, not after.
Chat mode
A mode where you talk without it building anything. Good for thinking out loud, asking how it would approach something, or asking it to explain what it's done, without spending a credit on a rebuild.
Select an element
Lets you click directly on the button or text in the preview and talk to it about THAT, instead of describing in words where it is. Saves misunderstandings and therefore credits.
Connect to GitHub
The button that pulls your code out of here and puts it into your GitHub account. Click it day one. It's the only thing that guarantees your work isn't held hostage inside this website.
Connect Supabase
Hooking up a real database, with user accounts and permissions. It's the step that turns a demo open to anyone into something that can touch real data.
Publish / Deploy
Takes your app out of the preview and gives it a real internet address. Careful: publishing isn't the same as securing. A published app with no accounts can be seen by anyone with the link.
Remix / duplicate the project
Makes a copy to experiment with. Before a big overhaul, duplicate and work on the copy: if it goes wrong, you delete the copy and nothing happened.
The credit counter
Check it before starting each session. Working without knowing how many attempts you have left is like driving without checking the fuel gauge.
daily: One long, thought-out message, not five short ones. It's the habit that saves the most money and improves the result the most. Write it outside, on paper or in a notes app, and paste the whole message once it's complete.
Always ask it to tell you what it understood BEFORE building. Two lines from it save you three rebuilds. When you see its assumptions written out, you'll see what you hadn't spelled out.

Test by breaking, not by admiring. Submitting the form empty, typing where you shouldn't, and uploading a huge file teaches you more in two minutes than half an hour checking whether the colors match. And those are exactly the bugs your customer would find.
Correct by pointing at the screen, not describing it. Use the select tool and click the element. 'This button' works much better than 'the blue button at the bottom of the second form'.
Leave the look for last. Colors and fonts change in a minute once everything else works. Fighting with them at the start burns the credits you need to get the app doing what it's supposed to do.
Connect GitHub day one and Supabase before touching real data. Two buttons, and they're the difference between a toy and something that can grow.

Know when to stop. Once you've had three messages in a row with no progress, don't send a fourth: go back to the previous version in the history and rethink the brief from a different angle. Insisting on a path that isn't working is how you burn through a whole day's credits.

templates.name: The initial brief that avoids the generic app
templates.what: This is the first message, the long one. It's designed so that Lovable barely has to assume anything, because whatever it assumes, it's going to assume wrong. It works equally well for a company website, a data-collection form, an internal dashboard, or a small tool for your team.
templates.how: 1) Fill in the blanks in a notes app, not on the website: that way you don't spend credits while you're thinking. 2) Be specific about 'who's using it': age and device change the design decisions. 3) Leave the last two sections as they are: asking for a summary before building and the things you DON'T want yet are the two that avoid the most headaches. 4) Paste the whole message at once. 5) When it replies, read its assumptions before letting it continue.
fill: WHAT IT IS
One sentence. If you need two, it's two apps
WHO USES IT
Who, what age, and from phone or computer. Changes the entire design
WHAT IT CAN DO
Three things maximum, in order of importance. Everything else for the second version
WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE
Two colors and little else. No animations or gradients at the start
WHAT YOU DON'T WANT YET
Accounts and payments out of the first version: they add complexity and can come later
templates.code:
I want to build a simple web app. I'll describe the whole thing before
you start, and I want you to build it all at once, not in pieces.

WHAT IT IS: [ONE SENTENCE]

WHO USES IT: [WHO, WHAT AGE, FROM PHONE OR COMPUTER]

WHAT THEY SEE ON ARRIVAL: [THE FIRST SCREEN, DESCRIBED]

WHAT IT CAN DO, in order of importance:
1. [THE MAIN THING]
2. [THE SECOND THING]
3. [THE THIRD THING]

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT: [WHAT THEY SEE AND WHAT YOU SEE]

HOW I WANT IT TO LOOK: clean, with white space, large legible text, and
working well on mobile. Colors: [TWO COLORS].
No animations or gradients.

IN ENGLISH: all screen text in professional English, including buttons,
notices, and error messages.

TWO THINGS I DON'T WANT YET: don't set up user registration or
passwords, and don't connect payments. We'll look at that later.

Before building anything, tell me in five lines what you understood
needs to be done and what you had to assume because I didn't tell you.
Wait for me to confirm.

templates.name: The list of corrections sent all at once
templates.what: After testing your app you'll have five or six things wrong. Sending them one at a time costs five or six credits and also increases the chance that fixing one breaks another. This message groups them together and also includes three checks that are almost always missing from a first version.
templates.how: 1) Test the whole app and write down the bugs on paper as you find them, without fixing anything yet. 2) Test it on mobile too. 3) Write each bug in two parts: what happens and what should happen. 4) Paste the message. 5) When it's done, check it yourself: don't trust it just because it says it's done.
fill: WHAT HAPPENS
What you see, exactly. 'Nothing happens when I click submit'
WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN
The result you expected. Without this, it fixes whatever it thinks best
The three checks
Always leave these in: empty form, a sending indicator, and mobile
templates.code:
I've tested the app and found these things. Fix all of them in this
same change, not one at a time:

1. [WHAT HAPPENS] · It should [WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN]
2. [WHAT HAPPENS] · It should [WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN]
3. [WHAT HAPPENS] · It should [WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN]

Also, check these three things that I know tend to be missing, and fix
them if they are:

- That submitting the empty form shows a clear message in English
  saying which field is missing, instead of doing nothing.
- That while something is being sent, it's visible that it's happening,
  so nobody clicks the button three times in a row.
- That on mobile you don't have to zoom in to read or to tap.

Don't touch anything other than what I've asked for. When you're done,
tell me in two lines what you changed.

templates.name: The security check before showing it to anyone
templates.what: An app built in one afternoon is open by default: anyone with the link gets in, and often anyone can see everyone else's data. This message forces it to audit itself and tell you the truth before you put real data in there or hand the link to a client.
templates.how: 1) Send it once the app already does what it's supposed to. 2) Read its full response before letting it fix anything: you want to know what was there, not just have it patched over. 3) If it tells you user accounts need to be set up, do that before showing anyone real data. 4) Repeat this message every time you add a new screen that stores data.
fill: WHAT DATA IT STORES
Be literal: names, emails, phone numbers, files, amounts
WHO SHOULD SEE WHAT
The normal setup: each person only sees their own, and you see everything
templates.code:
Before showing this to anyone I want an honest security check.
Don't reassure me: I want to know what's actually open.

My app stores: [WHAT DATA IT STORES]
And should be visible to: [WHO SHOULD SEE WHAT]

Answer me in writing and in this order, before changing anything:

1. Can anyone with the link get in? Yes or no.
2. If someone gets in, can they see the data entered by ANOTHER person?
   Yes or no. This is the one I'm most worried about.
3. Is there any key, password, or token written inside the code that
   gets sent to the browser? If so, tell me which one and where.
4. What happens if someone submits the form a thousand times in a row?
5. What personal data am I storing and where does it physically end up?

After answering all five, and only then, tell me what needs to be set
up to lock it down, starting with the most serious issue, and how much
work each one is. Don't do it yet: I want to decide the order myself.

errors: The preview stays blank or keeps spinning

What it built has a bug that's preventing the page from rendering. It's one of the most common things on day one and doesn't mean you broke anything. Don't go looking at the code. Write to it: 'the preview is blank, tell me what error it's giving and fix it'; it can see the error even if you can't. If after two attempts it's still the same, don't try a third: go to the version history and revert to the previous one, which worked.

It wrote something the computer can't read. Happens mostly when you've asked for five big things in the same message. Paste the full error message into the chat, without summarizing or translating it, and add 'fix it and don't touch anything else'. Next time, split big requests into two: giant changes are the ones that fail the most.

You've used up today's messages. Nothing you built is lost and it's still there tomorrow. Use the break for something useful instead of getting frustrated: write down all your pending corrections on paper, and tomorrow send them in one numbered message instead of ten. You'll get further with those ten credits than with today's thirty.
Text comes out in Spanish even though you're prompting it in English

By default it may generate the interface in a language other than the one you want, and simply talking to it in your language isn't enough. Tell it explicitly and once and for all: 'all visible text in professional English, including buttons, notices, error messages, and help text'. When new screens later show up in the wrong language again, repeat it pointing at that screen.
Fixing one thing broke another thing that worked

It touched more than it needed to; happens mostly with visual changes that end up affecting logic. Tell it both things together in the same message: 'changing X broke Y; I want X the way I asked and Y back the way it was before'. If it gets more tangled after two attempts, revert to the previous version and ask for the change a different way.
Anyone with the link can see everyone's data

It's not a bug: it's what you asked for, even if you didn't know it. An app with no user accounts is open, and without row-level permissions, whoever logs in can see what someone else entered. Until you set up authentication and permissions, don't put a single real person's data in there. Fixed by connecting Supabase and asking for user accounts and access rules, and checked by logging in with two different accounts.
It deleted or changed a screen I hadn't touched

You asked for something in general terms ('clean up the design', 'simplify this') and it took that as a free pass. Go back to the previous version in the history and repeat the request with a narrower scope: 'change ONLY the contact screen; don't touch any other screen or file'.
It works in the preview but fails when published

It's almost always keys and variables: what was available inside the test environment isn't declared on the published site. Ask it explicitly: 'tell me what environment variables this app needs to work once published, where each one is declared, and what happens if one is missing'. It's the same problem any project has when it leaves the computer it was built on.

prompts.name: Decide whether Lovable is right for you before wasting an afternoon
prompts.prompt: Act as a senior developer who doesn't get a commission for selling me tools. I'm going to tell you what I want to build, and I want you to tell me the truth about whether Lovable is the right fit or is going to waste my time. First ask me whatever questions you need, one at a time, about who it's for, how many people will use it, what data it stores, whether it needs to connect with any software I already use, and what happens if it goes down on a Tuesday morning. Then answer me like this. One: tell me clearly whether this falls within what Lovable does well (screens, forms, lists, dashboards, pages that store data) or whether it strays into territory where it'll struggle (complicated business rules, integrations with legacy software, heavy concurrent volume, serious legal requirements), and what specific signal you're basing that on. Two: if it strays, tell me what I should use instead and how much it would cost, in dollars and in weeks, no sugarcoating. Three: if it fits, tell me what part of my idea is a reasonable first version and what part I should leave out even if it hurts. Four: tell me the three things about my case that are definitely going to cause problems and when they'll show up. Five: tell me how much this is going to cost me a month once it's running, counting the tool and everything needed behind it. Six: if your honest answer is that I should hire someone, tell me straight out. What I want to build is: [DESCRIBE IT IN PLAIN ENGLISH, AS YOU'D EXPLAIN IT TO A FRIEND].

prompts.name: Turn my idea into a brief Lovable will understand
prompts.prompt: I'm going to tell you what's in my head, out of order, and I want you to turn it into the brief I'm going to paste into Lovable. I don't know how to code, so don't make me decide anything technical: you decide and explain the decision in one line. Do it in this order. One: ask me at most five questions, one at a time, to fill in what's missing; focus on who's using it, from what device, what they need to be able to do, and what happens next. Two: write me the final brief, ready to copy and paste, with this structure: what it is, who uses it, what they see on arrival, what they can do (three things max, in order of importance), what happens next, what it looks like, and what I DON'T want in the first version. Three: highlight which of those decisions you made for me and why, so I can change them. Four: tell me which three things from my idea I put in the first version that should wait for the second, and what would happen if I insist on including them now. Five: add to the end of the brief the instruction that before building it should tell me what it understood and what it assumed. Six: warn me if any of what I want to store is personal data, because that changes what I need to set up before showing it to anyone. My idea is: [TELL IT HOWEVER IT COMES OUT, UNORGANIZED].

prompts.name: Security audit before handing the link to anyone
prompts.prompt: I have an app built with Lovable and I'm about to hand the link to real people. Before that I want an honest audit, not a reassuring report. Answer all of this in writing before changing a single line, because I want to know what was there, not just have it patched over. One: can anyone with the link get in? Two: if two different people use the app, can one see the data entered by the other? Answer yes or no and show me what you're basing that on. Three: is there any key, token, or password written into the code that reaches the browser? If so, tell me which, where it is, and what someone could do with it. Four: what happens if someone submits the form a thousand times in a minute? Five: what personal data am I storing, where does it physically end up, and how long does it stay there? Six: if tomorrow I wanted to delete all of a specific person's data because they asked me to, could I, and how? Once you've answered all six, and only then, give me a list of what needs fixing ordered by severity, saying for each one how much work it is and what breaks while you fix it. Don't fix anything yet: I want to decide the order myself. My app stores: [WHAT DATA] and it's going to be used by: [WHO].

prompts.name: Get the project out of Lovable without getting stuck
prompts.prompt: I have an app running on Lovable and I want to understand exactly how dependent I am on this tool before I put in more hours. I don't necessarily want to leave: I want to know that I could. Answer me like this. One: tell me which parts of my project are standard code that any programmer could pick up and continue, and which parts depend on something Lovable-specific that would stay here. Two: tell me step by step what I'd have to do to take the whole project to my own GitHub account and run it on my own, including what I'd need to install and what outside services I'd need to sign up for separately. Three: tell me approximately what it would cost per month to run it outside of here. Four: tell me what would break on moving day and what would need to be rebuilt. Five: tell me what I should be doing NOW to make that move easy the day I want it, even if that's two years from now. Six: if your honest answer is that at my scale this isn't worth worrying about, tell me that too. My app is: [DESCRIBE IT] and it's been running for: [HOW LONG].

prompts.name: Rescue a project that broke and I don't know why
prompts.prompt: My Lovable app was working and now it isn't. I don't know how to code and I don't want theory: I want it working again. Walk me through it step by step, one thing at a time, starting with the lowest-risk option. Before proposing any changes, ask me whatever you need: what was the last thing I asked for before it stopped working, what message exactly shows on screen, whether the preview is blank or shows a written error, and whether the bug also shows up on mobile. Once you have that clear, tell me: one, what happened in one sentence of plain English; two, whether the sensible move is to revert to a previous version in the history or try fixing it in place, and why that option over the other; three, if we revert, exactly what work of mine gets lost, so I can decide with the facts in front of me; four, the concrete steps, telling me where to click; five, how I check it's fixed, with a test that takes less than a minute; six, what I should do from now on so this doesn't catch me again. And tell me too, without me having to ask, whether there's a risk that data people had entered was lost. The last thing I asked for was: [WHAT YOU ASKED FOR]. What's showing now is: [WHAT SHOWS].

words: Prompt
What you write to it. It's the brief, in plain everyday language. Here it works best long and specific, not a loose sentence.
Credit
What you spend every time you send it an instruction. You don't pay by time: you pay by message, which is why it pays to bundle corrections together.
Preview
The right half of the screen, with your app actually working. You can click it and fill it in: it's not a picture.
Publish / Deploy
Taking it out of the preview and giving it a real internet address. Publishing isn't securing: without accounts, it stays open to whoever has the link.
Repository
Your project's folder with its entire history, on GitHub. It's your backup and your guarantee against being stuck here.
Supabase
The service Lovable uses to store data and set up user accounts. It's what turns a demo into something that can touch real data.
Authentication
The username and password system. Until you set it up, your app can be seen by anyone with the link.
Version history
The list of saved states of your project. It's the real undo button for when a change has made three things worse.
Responsive
The screen adapting to a phone's width without forcing you to zoom. Checked on an actual phone, not by imagining it.
Environment variable
A key or setting that lives outside the code. It's the usual cause of something working in the preview and failing once published.
matters: The long brief, written out before sending the first message. It's half the work and the only thing separating an app that resembles what you wanted from a generic one. Whatever you don't explain, it's going to assume, and it's going to assume wrong.

Connect GitHub day one. It's thirty seconds and it's the only thing that guarantees that whatever happens with this tool, your work keeps existing and someone else can continue it. People remember this once they no longer can.
Don't put in real people's data until you have accounts and permissions, and check it by logging in with two different accounts. A freshly built app is open by default and nobody's going to warn you.

Bundle corrections into one message. Every instruction costs a credit and increases the chance of breaking something that worked. Five 'make it bigger now' messages are the most expensive beginner mistake.
ignore: Colors, fonts, and general look during the first sessions. They change in a minute at the end, and fighting with them at the start burns the credits you need to get the app working.
The code tab. You don't need to understand it to work this way, and looking at it now just causes stress. The moment will come, and it'll be when you want to change something very specific.

Custom domains, payments, multiple languages, and anything that starts with 'and also'. Each of those is a whole topic on its own. Cramming them into the first afternoon is the surest way to finish nothing.
